extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and documenting subject‑matter eligibility analyses under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including when to use a streamlined pathway, how to identify judicial exceptions, and how to formulate rejections. Intended to direct examiner reasoning, required explanations, examples, and recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that merely add insignificant activity beyond a judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering, printing/downloading generated menus, cutting hair after determining hairstyle) do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception and are examples of insignificant computer implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., storing data added to a claim that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information. When present, treat these limitations as potential examples of insignificant extra-solution activity and articulate why they fail to integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link the use of a judicial exception to a particular field of use or technological environment (i.e., 'limiting to the Internet', 'to cellular telephones', 'to power-grid data') do not by themselves amount to significantly more than the exception and cannot integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance gives many case examples (e.g., Parker v. Flook; Diamond v. Diehr contrast; Affinity Labs; Mayo; Bilski; FairWarning; Intellectual Ventures; Ultramercial; buySAFE) showing that token or incidental field‑of‑use/technology restrictions are insufficient. Examiners should treat the terms 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeably, consider overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity, and explain in the rejection why such limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A streamlined analysis may be used when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (for example, because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined (Pathway A) analysis must yield the same result as the full Alice/Mayo test; it is a tool for examination efficiency, not a way to avoid a finding that would result from full analysis. If there is doubt whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception, the full analysis (Alice/Mayo) should be conducted. The record may simply reflect eligibility by the absence of an eligibility rejection or a clarifying remark when Pathway A is used (see MPEP § 2106.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident (use of streamlined pathway)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that, when viewed as a whole, clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception and therefore have self-evident eligibility do not require a full Alice/Mayo analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include complex manufactured industrial products/processes with meaningful limitations (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using mathematical relationships) or nature-based products that obviously do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., an artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral). Such claims can be eligible under Pathway A. However, claims that would fail Step 2B of the full analysis are not suitable for streamlined analysis (see MPEP § 2106.06(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that clearly improve technology or computer functionality may not be directed to an abstract idea and thus may avoid the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Enfish (self-referential table) and McRO (automatic lip synchronization) as examples where improvements enabled eligibility. If the improvement is a 'close call' (e.g., BASCOM filtering cases), the full analysis should be performed. Examiners may reasonably apply Pathway A, B, or C depending on whether they view the claim as presenting a clear improvement or requiring further analysis (see MPEP § 2106.06(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and review the record as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be grounded in the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent, and examiners must review the entire record (specification, claims, prosecution history, relevant case law, prior art) before concluding eligibility or ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training materials and examples explain policy but do not themselves serve as a legal basis for rejection. Examiners must make claim-by-claim determinations (dependent claims may differ from independent claims). If a claim is more likely than not ineligible (Step 1 NO and/or Step 2B NO), formulate a prima facie rejection that clearly and specifically explains the basis so applicants can respond (see MPEP § 2106.07). Examiners should also perform a complete examination under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, etc.) and state all non-cumulative reasons/bases in the first Office action in line with compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identify the judicial exception and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under Step 2A Prong One must identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited in the claim and explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim 'describes' but does not 'expressly set forth' the judicial exception, the rejection must explain what subject matter the limitations describe and provide a reasoned rationale why it is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, the rejection should identify how the recited concept fits within the groupings enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) (mathematical concepts, mental processes, methods of organizing human activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — identify additional elements and evaluate integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under Step 2A Prong Two must identify any additional elements beyond the judicial exception (point to specific claim features/limitations/steps) and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluation must explain that (1) there are no additional elements, or (2) the claim as a whole (looking at additional elements individually and in combination) does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application, using the considerations in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in this analysis, even if they appear to be well-understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — explain why additional elements do or do not amount to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Step 2B rejection must explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner concludes that certain elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activities, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing using one of the four options specified in Subsection III (e.g., factual findings, citations, reasoning — see MPEP § 2106.07(a) for required support). The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case of ineligibility and provide applicant adequate notice to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for Step 1 rejections (statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is determined not to fall within a statutory category (Step 1: NO), the rejection must explain why the claim does not fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should follow the discussion and standards in MPEP § 2106.03 when drafting Step 1 rejections, and provide clear, specific explanations in the Office action to enable effective applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant responses and subsequent prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must carefully consider all of applicant’s arguments and evidence when evaluating responses to an eligibility rejection and either withdraw the rejection if properly challenged or provide a rebuttal in the next Office action if the rejection is maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This obligation is discussed in MPEP § 2106.07(b). Examiners must ensure the record reflects reasoned consideration of applicant submissions and, when maintaining a rejection, provide a written rebuttal addressing applicant's points.
